evidence.quote:
For every fixed integer $K\ge2$, there is a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction mapping a $3$SAT formula $\varphi$ to a pair $(G,k)$, where $G$ is an explicit finite simple undirected unweighted graph and $k\ge1$ is a binary-encoded integer, such that $$\begin{aligned}
 \varphi\text{ satisfiable}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       \operatorname{OPT}_{\rm uncut}(G)\le k,\\
 \varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       \operatorname{OPT}_{\rm uncut}(G)>Kk.
 \end{aligned}$$ For each fixed $K$, the graph size, full construction work, and bit complexity are polynomial in the bit length of $\varphi$. All constants are effective; no advice or oracle is supplied to the reduction.

exclusions.query: An efficient optimizer for arbitrary graph instances
exclusions.reason: The main result is an approximation-hardness reduction; it does not supply an optimizer.

evidence.quote: This does not assert uniformity of one form conditional on previously revealed forms.

exclusions.query: Uniformity of a form conditional on previously revealed hints
exclusions.reason: The smoothness bound concerns the joint collection conditional on the first question.

hypotheses.statement:
For every fixed integer $K\ge2$, there is a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction mapping a $3$SAT formula $\varphi$ to a pair $(G,k)$, where $G$ is an explicit finite simple undirected unweighted graph and $k\ge1$ is a binary-encoded integer, such that $$\begin{aligned}
 \varphi\text{ satisfiable}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       \operatorname{OPT}_{\rm uncut}(G)\le k,\\
 \varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       \operatorname{OPT}_{\rm uncut}(G)>Kk.
 \end{aligned}$$ For each fixed $K$, the graph size, full construction work, and bit complexity are polynomial in the bit length of $\varphi$. All constants are effective; no advice or oracle is supplied to the reduction.

For every fixed real $C>1$, minimum $2$CNF clause deletion is NP-hard to approximate within factor $C$. In particular, a deterministic polynomial-time $C$-approximation would imply $\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}$.

The map $a\mapsto\operatorname{ev}_a$, where $\operatorname{ev}_a(b)=b(a)$, is a bijection from $A$ onto the odd frequencies of $D(A)$. If $\pi:A\to A'$ is affine and $\pi^*:D(A')\to D(A)$ is pullback, then its dual sends $\operatorname{ev}_a$ to $\operatorname{ev}_{\pi(a)}$.

For every fixed rational $\zeta>0$, there is a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from $3$SAT to a nonempty explicit list of equations $x_i+x_j+x_k=b$ over $\mathbb F_2$, with uniform sampling from the list, such that satisfiable inputs admit an assignment satisfying at least $1-\zeta$ of the list and unsatisfiable inputs admit none satisfying more than $3/4$. The list length and the full bit complexity are polynomial for fixed $\zeta$.

There is an effectively specified constant $c<1$ such that every finite game with at most eight first-player answers, at most two second-player answers, and value at most $11/12$ has $r$-fold repeated value at most $c^r$ for all integers $r\ge0$. The same $c$ works for all question distributions and all question-set sizes.

For any choice of labels $a_\xi\in A_\xi$, the evaluation proofs $f_\xi(P)=P(a_\xi)$ satisfy $\varepsilon_j\le b_j$ for $j=1,2,3$. In fact, $$\varepsilon_1\le 2\sigma,\qquad
 \varepsilon_2\le2\delta+2\eta,\qquad
 \varepsilon_3=|\mathcal C|^{-1}.$$

Assume $\varepsilon_1\le Jb_1$ and $\varepsilon_2\le Jb_2$, and use [eq:smoothing-parameters]–[eq:hermite-cutoff-choice]. For every $m,n\ge2$, $$\begin{aligned} \mathbb E\lVert h\rVert_{2,x}^2&\ge\frac34,\label{eq:gradient-lower}\\ \mathbb E\lVert(I-\Pi_c)h\rVert_{2,x}^2&\le\frac1{16},\label{eq:c-tail}\\ \mathbb E\lVert(I-\Pi_B)h\rVert_{2,x}^2&\le\frac1{32},\label{eq:B-tail}\\ \mathbb E\langle L,h\rangle_x=\mathbb E\lVert L\rVert_{2,x}^2&\ge\frac12, \qquad \mathbb E\lVert L\rVert_{2,x}^2\le\sigma^{-2}. \label{eq:L-energy} \end{aligned}$$

Fix $J$ and the constants [eq:smoothing-parameters]–[eq:hermite-cutoff-choice]. For every $m,n\ge2$ and every finite weighted family of folded proofs satisfying $\varepsilon_j\le Jb_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, the field $L$ from [eq:low-degree-field] has Fourier row degree at most $Rm$ and Gaussian degree at most $s$, satisfies [eq:L-energy], and obeys $$\label{eq:correlation-lower} \mathbb E\mathfrak d_X(L)\ge\frac1{4T}.$$ All constants preceding $m,n$ are uniform in their values and in the affine alphabets.

Let $Q_x^Y$ select any collection of complete exact-mask/Hermite components with $|I|\le s$, using only $x,Y,I,S$. For a fixed axis $i$ let $q_{x,i}^Y$ be the maximum odd row coefficient of $Q_x^Yh_x$ in $r=(i,x_{-i})$, with the other rows and $c$ held fixed. Then $$\label{eq:projector-maximum}
 \mathbb E\mathbb E_{x\in Y}q_{x,i}^Y
 \le C_0\left(\mathbb E\mathbb E_{x\in X}a_{x,i}^2\right)^{1/2},
 \qquad C_0=4^M\binom{N+s}{s}.$$ The estimate is valid for every weighted distribution of proof indices.

If no assignment satisfies more than $3/4$ of the equation list, the ordinary equation-versus-variable game has value at most $11/12$. Consequently its ordinary $r$-fold repetition has value at most $c^r$, for the effective universal constant $c<1$ of Theorem 5, for every $r\ge0$.

Suppose no assignment satisfies more than $3/4$ of the equation list. For every $q\ge0$ and $t\ge t_0\ge1$, the value of the game with $q$ affine hints is at most $$\label{eq:hint-bound} \bigl(1-2^{-q}(1-c)\bigr)^{t_0}.$$ The bound also applies to strategies using arbitrary independent shared or private randomness. In particular, for fixed $q$ and any prescribed rational $s>0$, an effective choice of $t_0$ makes the bound strictly less than $s$, simultaneously for every $t\ge t_0$, every equation-list size, and every completeness parameter in Theorem 4.

Fix any actual first question $U$, integers $d\ge1$ and $t\ge t_0\ge1$, and draw the remaining outer sample conditional on $U$. Draw $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ independently and uniformly from $D(A_V)$. Then $$\label{eq:smoothness-bound}
 \operatorname{TV}\left(\mathcal L\bigl((\pi_e^*L_1,\ldots,\pi_e^*L_d)\mid U\bigr),
                 \operatorname{Unif}(D(A_U)^d)\right)
 \le\frac12\sqrt{(2^{4dt_0}-1)\frac{t_0^2}{t}}.$$ The bound is uniform in $U$ and the equation list, including repeated variable names and zero-dimensional local alphabets. For fixed $d,t_0$ and positive rational $\Delta$, an effective integer $t\ge t_0$ makes the right-hand side strictly less than $\Delta$.

Because [eq:smoothness-bound] is uniform in $U$, it may be averaged over any distribution of $U$ and any extra randomness independent of the outer sample. In particular, if a bounded statistic is chosen as a function of $U$ and some of the pulled-back forms, one may apply Lemma 14 to the joint collection of all forms used by that statistic. For a statistic bounded in absolute value by $B$, the change in expectation is at most $2B$ times the displayed total-variation bound. This does not assert uniformity of one form conditional on previously revealed forms.

For every fixed integer $J\ge20$, effective choices of constants give a four-test comparison system with the following properties. It is constructed from the uniform equation list in Theorem 4, for a fixed completeness error $\zeta>0$ chosen by the construction. Every test compares two bits in folded proof tables, and its contribution to cost is its failure probability divided by a positive rational budget $b_j$. In the YES case there are proof tables of cost at most $4$; in the NO case every collection of proof tables has cost greater than $J$. Alphabet sizes are bounded by effective constants depending only on $J$, and all local numerical parameters depend only on $J$.

coverage.checked_domain: Exhaustive ordered endpoint pairs and relations on n=1,2; all ordered demand lists of length at most 2 with multiplicities 0,1,2 and total at most 3; all original endpoint assignments. Additional n=3 shared-endpoint boundary cases.
coverage.oracle_basis: Candidate minimizes uncut cost over every fresh internal assignment; independent oracle enumerates endpoint signs and counts violated demands directly using exact integers.
